extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, researchers and policymakers interested in peer review quality and evidence-based editorial practices (biomedical journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials evaluating interventions intended to improve the quality of peer review for biomedical journal manuscripts. Focuses on types of interventions, measured outcomes, trial design and synthesis methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training (intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Training, which included training or mentoring programs for peer reviewers to provide instructional support for appropriately evaluating important components of manuscript submissions. These interventions directly target the ability of peer reviewers to appropriately evaluate the quality of the manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes structured workshops with journal editors, self-taught training packages, mentoring (new reviewers discussing reviews with senior reviewers), and feedback (reviewers receiving editor's rating of their review). RCT evidence in the review showed training did not improve quality of peer review reports; heterogeneity across studies was high. One study reported training increased recommendations to reject. Consider risk of attrition bias in training trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition of peer reviewers for specific tasks (statistical peer reviewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition of peer reviewers for specific tasks or with specific expertise such as adding a statistical peer reviewer, whose main task is to detect the misuse of methods or misreporting of statistical analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCT evidence (two trials from same journal/team) showed adding a statistical peer reviewer improved the quality of the final manuscript (combined SMD 0.58; 95% CI 0.19 to 0.98). External validity may be limited because evidence came from a single journal and team; replication in other contexts is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer reviewers’ use of a checklist (reporting guideline checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviewers’ use of a checklist, such as reporting guideline checklists, to evaluate the quality of the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include checklists based on reporting guideline items (e.g., CONSORT items). RCT evidence in the review did not show an effect of checklist use on the quality of the final manuscript (combined SMD 0.19; 95% CI –0.22 to 0.61). Trials were limited in number and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review (intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Open” peer review process, whereby peer reviewers are informed that their name would be revealed to the authors, other peer reviewers, and/or the public. The purpose of these approaches is to increase transparency and thus increase the accountability of existing peer reviewers to produce good-quality peer reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types evaluated: open to other peer reviewers, open to authors, open to the public (web-posting). Meta-analysis found open peer review increased the quality of the peer review report (combined SMD 0.14; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.24), decreased recommendations to reject (OR 0.56; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.94) with heterogeneity for rejection rate, and did not significantly change time spent on reviews overall. Subgroup analysis by type showed no clear differences. Potential selection/participation biases (subjects declining) noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blinded/masked peer review (intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Blinded”/masked peer review, whereby peer reviewers are blinded to author names and affiliation. Author names and/or potentially identifying credentials are removed from manuscripts sent for peer review so as to remove or minimize peer reviewer biases that arise from knowledge of and assumptions about author identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analysis did not show clear effects of blinding on quality of peer review reports (SMD 0.12; 95% CI –0.12 to 0.36) or rejection rate (OR 0.77; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.50); substantial heterogeneity existed. The goal of blinding is to favor objective and fair review, but fairness is hard to evaluate; trials faced practical problems such as unintentional discovery of author identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other interventions to increase speed of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Any other types of interventions identified aimed at increasing the speed of the peer review process (examples: first asking peer reviewers whether they agree to review versus directly sending the manuscript; calling peer reviewers versus sending manuscript; early editorial screening of manuscripts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes were heterogeneous and incompletely reported, preventing pooled meta-analysis in this category. One RCT found early editorial screening decreased mean duration. Interventions differ in mechanism and measured endpoints, so results are context-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final manuscript quality (outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final manuscript quality (i.e., revised manuscript after all peer review assessments and rounds). Several scales were used to assess manuscript quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example instrument: Manuscript Quality Assessment Instrument — a 34-item scale, each item scored from 1 to 5, evaluating whether research is described with sufficient detail and clarity; organized by article sections (Title/Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, General). Other measures assessed completeness of reporting using reporting guideline items (e.g., CONSORT). A high score indicates a high quality manuscript. Note: final manuscript quality depends on authors’ revisions and editorial enforcement as well as peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of the peer review report (outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of the peer review report, measured by scales such as the Review Quality Instrument or editor routine quality rating scales. A high score indicates a high quality peer review report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review Quality Instrument (latest version) is based on eight items: importance, originality, methodology, presentation, constructiveness of comments, substantiation of comments, interpretation of results, and a global item; items scored on a 5-point scale. Reported inter-rater agreement: K = 0.83 for agreement on items, and mean total score inter-rater reliability K = 0.31. Editors’ routine scales and validity/minimally important differences may be questionable; choice of what constitutes appropriateness is debatable and may vary by editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection rate (outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejection rate defined as recommendation by peer reviewers about whether or not the reviewed manuscripts should be rejected from publication in the journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a proxy to assess peer reviewer decision behavior; relationship between recommendation to reject and actual quality of published study is unclear. Heterogeneity in its interpretation and drivers (topic interest, reviewer subjectivity) should be considered when using rejection rate as an outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time spent on peer review (outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time spent on the peer review as reported by peer reviewers. The time spent is important to provide an evaluation of the burden and possible cost of the peer review process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in minutes; used to assess reviewer burden and resource implications of interventions. Open peer review trials did not show a clear overall difference in reviewer time (combined MD 0.18; 95% CI –0.06 to 0.43) though heterogeneity existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall duration of the peer review process (outcome)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall duration of the peer review process (time from submission to decision or completion of review rounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate interventions aimed at accelerating review; outcome reporting was heterogeneous across trials, limiting pooling and clear inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility/inclusion criteria for trials in the review
rubrics_metrics.description: Include randomized controlled trials (RCTs), whatever the unit of randomization (manuscript or peer reviewers), evaluating any interventions aimed at improving the quality of peer review for biomedical publications regardless of publication language. Exclude RCTs evaluating the presence and effect of peer reviewer bias on the outcome (such as positive outcome bias) and exclude non-randomized studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No limitation on date or language. Duplicate publications collated. Unit of randomization (peer reviewer/manuscript) and trial design affect applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of randomization (design consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unit of randomization could be peer reviewers, manuscripts, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chosen unit affects trial design, analytic approach and applicability/generalizability. Randomizing reviewers vs manuscripts has different implications for contamination, clustering and external validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of bias assessment (Cochrane domains)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk of bias within each RCT was assessed by the following domains of the Cochrane Collaboration risk of bias tool: selection bias (methods for random sequence generation and allocation concealment), detection bias (blinding of outcome assessors) and attrition bias (incomplete outcome data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performance bias (blinding of participants and providers) was not assessed because blinding was often impossible in this context. Each domain rated low/high/unclear. As recommended, blinding of outcome assessors and incomplete outcome data domains were assessed at the outcome level. When risk of bias was unclear, contact authors for clarification. Consider detection bias low if peer reviewers were unaware of study hypothesis or outcome assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction and handling (methods standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized data extraction: record means and standard deviations for continuous outcomes; derive them from reported data if not provided following Cochrane handbook recommendations. For dichotomous outcomes record counts of manuscripts and rejections. For studies with multiple intervention groups follow Cochrane recommendations to combine groups or select pairs. Extract outcomes reported as primary or latest time point to avoid selective inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When necessary, extract data from figures using DigitizeIt and contact authors for missing data. Avoid combining final value and change-from-baseline scores as SMDs. Ensure transparent, pre-specified extraction forms and dual independent extraction with consensus procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect measures and synthesis methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use odds ratios (ORs) for binary outcomes (rejection rate) and standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes (quality scores), because trials used different scoring systems. Use random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian and Laird model) due to diversity of interventions and settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess heterogeneity by forest plots, Cochran’s Q (homogeneity test), and I^2 statistic. Perform subgroup analyses when appropriate (example: intensity/type of open peer review). Use Review Manager or equivalent software. Interpret pooled SMDs with attention to clinical/editorial relevance and heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple intervention groups and outcome reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When studies reported several results for selected outcomes (e.g., multiple scales or time points), retrieve the result reported as the primary outcome in the manuscript or the final/latest time point. For multi-arm trials, combine relevant intervention groups or control groups per Cochrane guidance or select an appropriate pair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach avoids selective inclusion of results and maintains comparability across trials. Be explicit about choices and follow Cochrane Handbook methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication bias and small study effects assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess publication bias and small study effect by visual inspection of funnel plots when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret funnel plots cautiously when the number of included trials is small. Acknowledge limitations in detecting reporting bias with few RCTs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and validity of outcomes (construct validity considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of relevant outcomes is difficult: outcomes assessed were mainly editors’ subjective assessments or validated scales to assess review/manuscript quality. The criteria to consider the appropriateness of a peer review report can be debatable and vary by editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question the validity of some outcomes (e.g., editors’ routine scales) and the minimally important editorial difference. Recognize that rejection recommendations may not map directly to manuscript quality and that final manuscript quality depends on authors' and editors' actions. Use multiple complementary outcomes and explicitly justify their relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability and applicability considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of journals, peer reviewers and manuscripts will affect applicability of study results. Most RCTs were performed in a single journal, limiting generalizability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider journal culture, standard review procedures, sub-specialty context, and reviewer experience when applying trial results. Replication across diverse journals and contexts is necessary before broad implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical and ethical design constraints (blinding and participation biases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing study aims and procedures is difficult and sometimes impossible. For blinding interventions, unintentional discovery of author identity was reported; for open peer review, controversial opinions led to declining participation or non-completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and mitigate selection, performance and detection biases where possible; document and report participation/refusal rates and assess impact on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: clarify goals, definitions and need for experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The review recommends clarifying the goal of the peer review process, defining a good quality peer review report, and deciding which outcomes should be used. Evidence-based peer review needs development and further RCT experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial boards and decision-makers should weigh uncertainty, methodological shortcomings and practical challenges before implementing interventions. Additional well-performed trials across diverse settings are needed to strengthen the evidence base.
